newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan traders see Russia palladium talks in April.
newsitem.headline: Japan traders see Russia palladium talks in April.

text.p: Japan-Russia talks on 1997 palladium supply contracts are likely in April, although this year's first contracted deliveries will probably not arrive before May, Japanese traders said on Wednesday.
They added, however, that they expected Russia to resume spot market sales of the metals as soon as the export agency's yearly quota is approved, which could take place later this week.
Officials of the export agency, Almazjuvelirexport (Almaz), said last week the resumption of exports hinged on a resolution awaiting Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's signature.
Japanese traders said they had not yet received word from Almaz on when the annual contract talks, postponed since mid-December, would be held.
"We are still waiting, but even if Almaz comes to Japan in early April, the first deliveries under the contracts would be in May at earliest," said an official at a major Japanese bullion house.

Japan is the world's largest consumer and Russia the largest producer of palladium. Annual contract talks between the two sides have been delayed by political circumstances in Russia, including protracted wrangling over this year's budget.

The Japanese bullion house source added, however, that few Japanese would want contracted deliveries in April anyway, due to very high palladium prices in March. Contract prices are based on the average New York Mercantile Exchange palladium price in the previous month.

Palladium prices surged by one-third since the end of January, as the delay in the Japan-Russia talks fuelled heavy speculative buying. The spot price hit a nine-month high last week of $161 an ounce, although it later retraced, trading around $145 an ounce as of 0730 GMT on Wednesday.

Given the fact that Almaz has not even started negotiations with Japanese customers, the bullion house source said, there was even a possibility that the first contracted shipments would be postponed until June.
There was also talk in the market that Almaz's export quota this year would be reduced sharply from last year's levels.
"The question is whether Almaz will have enough of an export quota to meet Japanese demand," a trade house source said.
With no supply contracts yet for 1997, Japan's palladium traders have been forced since the beginning of the year to turn to the spot market to fill their requirements.
This did not, however, prevent them from importing large quantities of palladium, much of it of Russian origin but purchased through markets in Zurich and elsewhere.
Japan's palladium imports in January surged 224 percent from a year earlier to 8.156 tonnes, according to Finance Ministry data.
Makoto Tonoki, general manger at Tanaka Kikinzoku Kogyo K.K., estimated Japan's February imports would remain high at about nine tonnes. Monthly imports are usually about five to six tonnes.
Traders have also borrowed palladium to meet their needs, driving palladium ingot lease rates in Tokyo to three to four percent, up from about one percent at the end of last year.
"The consistently higher lease rates suggest that available metal supplies are tight," a trade house source said.
"Traders, who were wary of buying palladium at the recent high prices, were tending to borrow in the lease market," he said.
